Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights

We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights , well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming .

Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights .

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.

Today, weights are written by optimization , by custom networks trained to write them , or by compilers from formal programs . In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .

We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks . After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.

In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks .

In Weight-Space Programming , a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.

In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch . We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:

We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.

items.title: Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time
items.content:
The car that I drive is a 2014 Renault Latitude. It's not a fancy car by any means and is starting to show its age, but it gets me from point A to point B and does everything else reasonably well so I've never really had any reason to complain. When I bought the car, the previous owner asked me whether I wanted a "navigation map SD card" with it. They mentioned that the car apparently needs this SD card just to change the time on the clock, but I didn't really find that believable - not that they were lying to me, but perhaps they couldn't figure out how to enter the correct settings menu. After all, videos of similar head units online showed the menu with the clock settings option right there. Since the maps on the SD card were apparently very out of date and didn't function properly, I decided I didn't need it and the previous owner tossed it.

I didn't really miss it. The dashboard display did show a large "No maps found!" message taking up the majority of the display, but it didn't bother me too much. Like most other European countries, Estonia uses daylight saving time, and we recently switched from summer time (UTC+3) to "winter time" (UTC+2), which meant that the time displayed on the dashboard was out of sync by an hour. I dived into the settings menu, hoping to easily find the "Set time" option in there. That never happened. The menu where the "Set time" option should've been simply didn't have that option. I compared the menus with the ones in online videos, and the option was simply missing. There were two "Settings" buttons on the dash, and one of them worked but only let me change various Bluetooth and phonebook settings, with no time & date settings in sight. The second Settings button did not work whatsoever, instead showing a "No maps detected!" pop up message every time I pressed it. I must've spent an hour going through various menus, pressing various buttons or button combinations hoping to land in the correct menu, searching the web for information on this particular unit simply because I refused to believe that there was no option to change the time and I clearly must've been missing something obvious . Just RE it

Still in denial, I decided to fetch the firmware and dig into it, hoping to find some indication on how to open the correct settings menu. Luckily, I wasn't the first to embark on this journey and someone had already done some reverse engineering work on this particular unit ( https://github.com/andronedev/carminat-tomtom-live-re/blob/main/README.md ). While it was in French and seemingly heavily LLM-assisted, it did point me to the correct URLs for fetching the update files themselves. When extracted, the update files included a ttsystem file which turned out to be an ext3 filesystem containing the device's root filesystem, which was pretty much exactly what I was looking for. The unit itself (TomTom Carminat LIVE, codename beaumont ) is built around a Samsung S5P6440 SoC running TomTom's custom OS based on Linux 2.6.28.10. After reverse engineering it for a while, I came to the conclusion that the previous owner was completely correct. There was absolutely no way to enter the correct settings menu without a navigation SD card inserted. In fact, the menu definition pointing to the Settings applet was read from the SD card itself, and without one inserted containing the right menu definition, the unit didn't even know how to enter the Settings applet. This decision by TomTom (or Renault) is still baffling to me. What made things worse was that this needed to be a legitimate SD card. The system had DRM checks which rejected SD cards without the correct CID (a unique ID burned into the card) and files with signatures based on that specific CID, so I couldn't even copy the files to a blank SD card. I'm guessing the DRM was in place to prevent people from pirating maps. I don't want maps. I have a phone that I use for navigation. I just want to change the damn time. items.title: Brutal NIMBY Regulations Are Crushing the Kind of Solar Farms Researchers Say Are a Godsend for Local Ecology: "We're seeing a complete slowdown."
items.content:
By the end of the year, photovoltaics are expected to account for 10 percent of the world’s energy production, by which point it will have eclipsed even nuclear fission by sheer production capacity. As industrial supply chains make solar-generated electricity cheaper than ever before, a growing body of research indicates that solar farms are a net positive for many reasons — which makes recent anti-solar regulations all the more vexing.

New reporting by the Calgary Herald took a look at a 480-acre farm in southern Alberta, owned and operated by a man named Mark Owerko. Thanks to a transmission line located near his land, Owerko was situated in a prime area to establish a solar farm. After eight years, his property became a combination solar plant, apiary, and sheep farm.

That’s a winning combination, according to a paper published in the journal Environmental Research Letters . According to the study, allowing just two sheep per hectare to graze the grasses growing around photovoltaic installations improves the abundance of bees and beneficial beetles by 38 percent, driven mostly by an 83 percent increase in adjacent honey bee populations compared to solar farms mowed by hand.

As the paper’s lead author Leana Zoller told the Cornell Chronicle , “sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now.”

Despite what seems like a win-win both for Owerko and Alberta as a whole, the Herald notes that similar developments are nearly-impossible under the provinces’ current regulatory environment. That’s thanks in large part to restrictive rules around renewable energy on agricultural land meant to preserve “pristine viewscapes.”

As Owerko explains, his solar project was one of the very last approved by Alberta before the government imposed a seven-month moratorium on new wind and solar development.

“The moratorium drove power pricing into a ditch,” Owerko told the Herald . “In doing that, they chased away investment.”

“Everywhere else in the country, we see renewables being added to the grids at an accelerating pace and winning even in markets that are not specifically contracting for renewables,” director of the Business Renewables Centre of Canada Jorden Dy told the paper. “In Alberta, we’re seeing a complete slowdown.”

Whether Alberta can solve its renewable energy woes and restart solar investments in the province remains to be seen. Its regulatory regime is part of a strange trend emerging among some state- and provincial-level governments throughout North America , where restrictive and short-sighted regulations dictate which green energy developments are allowed on private land.

items.title: The advantages of mobile Linux over AOSP
items.content:
by Amos Batto (2026-10-19), License: CC BY 4.0 , Download: PDF , ODT

In response to my previous article asking, “ Will Linux phones become a viable alternative to the Android/iOS duopoly? ,” I received a torrent of comments at Hacker News , r/linux , r/Purism , r/mobilelinux , r/PINE64official , OSNews and on the forums at SailfishOS , Purism and PINE64 . There were a total of 660 comments and still counting, so people have a lot to say on the subject of Linux phones.

The vast majority of commentators don’t believe that Linux phones will ever crack the market stranglehold that Google and Apple currently hold over the mobile phone industry. However, many of the commentators argued that we already have a free/open source mobile Linux operating system in the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), which is the base on which Google and the phone manufacturers add their proprietary apps and services. They insisted that AOSP runs on a Linux kernel, so an AOSP phone already is a Linux phone. They asked why waste so much effort developing another mobile Linux operating system which won’t be nearly as good as AOSP. Other commentators argued that most people would never adopt Linux phones, because they are locked into one of the app ecosystems controlled by Google and Apple.

Here is a sample of the comments that the article received:

No, they [Linux phones] won’t become a viable alternative:

– Worse compatibility with the millions of Android apps already out there.

– Hardware vendors (outside Apple) all target Android.

– The usability of Android/iOS is far better than non-Android Linux phones.

– The security of non-Android Linux phones is in a bad state (e.g. lacking proper app sandboxing). Heck, even the Android emulation layers that some of these phones have, throw the strong Android sandbox model out of the window.

The answer is very obvious and it is AOSP. Even though Google is trying to close AOSP more (e.g. by not pushing source continuously to the AOSP Git repos and keeping QPR1/3 for themselves), it is still an open source system. Play Services can either be run sandboxed or emulated with microG. AOSP allows alternative systems to hit the ground running, you get great app compatibility, a tested security model, great usability, and support from hardware vendors, including vendors that are alternative friendly (used to be Pixel, now Motorola, Fairphone, etc.). If ever needed, AOSP could be forked and it would still be leagues ahead of non-Android Linux phones.

All the downsides that apply to AOSP-based systems (like things getting blocked by Play Integrity, unlockable bootloaders) also apply to non-Android Linux systems.

The difference is that there is already a great open source smartphone OS that works today , it’s AOSP.

The most effective path would be for the FLOSS ecosystem to pour their resources into making AOSP independent from Google. But instead people will just fork N half- or non-working solutions for reasons.

drnick responded to a previous comment on Hacker News:

> Play Services can either be run sandboxed or emulated with microG.

Play Services is absolutely not needed for a usable Android experience. I am running GrapheneOS without any Google crap and you could not pay me to do so.

Many bank apps, and apps to interact with official state services, usually depend on Play Services. Sometimes it is all banks in one’s country, so no, one can’t just “switch to another bank” as US Americans on HN often assume.

It’s not the phone or the os that’s the issue. It’s the app ecosystem. They own the store. In order to get a viable app store they need enough market share. In order to get market share they need a viable app store. Chicken meet Egg…I used a pinephone for hot minute and it was passable except I couldn’t use Slack, Teams, do banking, access my obsidian notes, etc.

No. They will never become a viable alternative to Android because those who want Android they [w]ill always prefer something like…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

items.title: WTF Ubuntu?
items.content:
In case you missed it: CVE-2026-98432 is a critical (CVSS 9.8)

bug in the Linux kernel's TCP code. It's been there since 2016, so virtually every Linux server on the planet

has it, and it can be hit remotely. Anthropic says it built a working exploit that gets root on a server.

Ubuntu still doesn't have a patch more than two weeks later.

Every supported release, LTS included, is listed as "Vulnerable".

Ubuntu's website promises "timely patches for critical vulnerabilities."

Ubuntu hasn't shipped the patch nine days after it was rated 9.8 and six days after a working root exploit.

Software is full of this blabber where words mean nothing. Ubuntu uses words like these:

"Timely." "Enterprise-grade." "Production grade." "Enterprise resilience. Developer velocity. Build with confidence on Ubuntu."

Somebody, or perhaps worse, some special team at Canonical is dedicated to writing these........

So I'm asking again... What the fuck, Ubuntu?

I'm moving all my servers off Ubuntu. I've completely lost trust in it.

On the desktop I always hated it anyway. On servers I mostly used it because it's the default

on most VPS providers, and I considered it the solid, no-drama LTS distro. Fuck that now.

I can't express how crazy this is. I didn't have time to migrate my services and data when I learned

about this, so I had to take all my servers that run Ubuntu offline.

Oh and btw, distros run by volunteers (Debian, Arch, Alpine...) hve shipped the fix. Meanwhile Ubuntu,

made by a company that sells security subscriptions, hasn't. This is true as of 2026-11-02 14:48 UTC.

items.title: A Decade of Kill Bugs
items.content:
On the morning of September 24th 2026, Endcrawl had a brief outage. I'd just typed:

Right away I blamed myself. Maybe I mistyped that number! Maybe my code had a signal handling bug. Maybe I don't understand Unix as well as I think I do. Maybe I'm an idiot!

As it turned out, the outage was caused by a bug in kill(1) .

This is really surprising. The kill program is 50 years old. Its spec is simple and stable. It's probably exercised a billion times a day.

A bug in kill was so surprising that, once I'd found it, I couldn't stop there. I needed to know how this bug came to be, and what had led the programmers so badly astray. When I eventually found the root cause, there was an even bigger surprise. It had led to not just one bug, but a whole series of kill bugs that shipped in Ubuntu 14, 16, 18, 22 and 24 LTS.

This post documents a decade of kill bugs, then makes some recommendations.

Back to the outage. I scrambled to put the fire out. After that came a surprise second fire. By the end of all this I was pretty demoralized. I was ready to accept that I'd made a dumb mistake and ready to get on with the work day. There was this nagging feeling though…

Remember that final scene in Burn After Reading?

"I don't f**king know either. I guess we learned not to do it again."

"Although I'm f**ked if I know what we did..."

What had just happened? Was I about to be hit with a third outage? How could I be sure?

An outage not understood is an outage that happens again. That nagging feeling I had was a call to understand. With a sigh, I put all my other work on hold and started a proper post mortem.

Let's examine the command that caused the outage:

The negative number here is a process group identifier , or pgid for short. A pgid is like a pid, but identifies a group of related processes. By convention, killing a positive number sends a signal to a single process, while killing a negative number signals all processes in that process group.

I was attempting to cancel a big Endcrawl 7k test render. A normal person would have killed one of the processes involved and let failures cascade to the others. But killing the whole group simultaneously strikes me as cleaner.

Process group signaling isn't some exotic operation. You use it all the time. Every time you ^C a command, the tty sends SIGINT to the foreground process group. Interactive shells run all but the simplest commands in a new process group, which among other things makes job control possible.

Process group signaling is in fact an awesome Unix innovation. I love it so much I added it to daemontools , where svc -+h now avoids orphans in a multiprocess service bounce.

At any rate, imagine my surprise when the command didn't just kill those render processes, but killed all processes on the machine save one!

Here's the relevant snippet from procps 4.0.4 , the provider of /bin/kill in Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. Can you spot the bug?

opterr = 0 ; /* suppress errors on -123 */

while (( i = getopt_long ( argc , argv , "l::Ls:hVq:" , longopts , & optindex )) != - 1 )

xwarnx ( _ ( "invalid argument %c" ), optopt );

/* Special case for signal digit negative

if ( ! execute_kill (( pid_t ) pid , signo , use_sigqueue , sigval ))

My initial guess was wrong. There's no underflow or overflow bug with -1490947 .

Notice we're in the unrecognized option switch case. Here's what getopt(3) says about unrecognized options:

By default, getopt() prints an error message on standard error, places the erroneous option character in optopt, and returns '?' as the function result.

Aha. The optopt variable only holds the first character after the dash, not the whole negative pid. When character 1 is subtracted from character 0 we get a pid of -1 . What happens when you kill pid -1 ? Bad things :

If pid equals -1, then sig is sent to every process for which the calling process has permission to send signals, except for process 1 (init).

This ran as root, so the misparsing of -1490947 as -1 killed…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

The New York Times sued Brave, the 11-year-old, privacy-focused browser company, on Monday, alleging it scraped the outlet’s copyrighted content and unlawfully distributed it to customers the suit names as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere.

Separately on Monday, the Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel filed a similar lawsuit. Both were brought in federal court in Manhattan.

The New York Times, which has also sued OpenAI and Perplexity over similar claims, likens Brave to a “supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content” for AI companies.

“In this way, Brave acts both like a burglar that misappropriates the content of publishers, and an AI ‘fence’ that sells stolen content to third parties,” the suit reads. It says Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages using an unidentified crawler, leaving publishers unable to block it.

The suit also targets a Brave browser feature that bypasses paywalls and the company’s practice of blocking publishers’ ads while selling its own.

Founded in 2015, Brave has raised roughly $250 million to date, according to private-market trackers. The Times seeks an injunction and damages.

Brave did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

총수, 의장 검찰 총원해서 조져 놓다가 사면을 해놓으니까 버릇이 안좋아 진건지 아니면 반도체좀 했다고 뭐가 된양인지 모르겠다만

앞으로 대한민국에서도 여당과 야당 합작으로 대기업 총수, 의장 사법처리하고 사면하지않고 만기 출소하는 케이스가 단 한 번이라도 나와서 명확하게 그 선례를 남겨놔야한다는게 내 생

items.title: Why did you choose the nix you nix?
items.content:
I don't which nix is good and at this point I'm afraid I need to ask.

(I suspect that Snix , Tvix , and others aren't intended for general use… but I might be wrong?)

Determinate Nix is the "corporate" version. It's run by big names in the Nix ecosystem but there's perennial concerns about them not upstreaming improvements, trying to shove features in, whatever. I don't know if it has any compelling benefits over cppnix.

Lix I like because it feels like they're trying to fix a lot of the papercuts that are involved in the ecosystem, untangle the gnarly codebase, and so on. AFAIK there are no incompatibilities between it and cppnix unless you do weird stuff.

Guix has the advantage of using a proper language and first class home-manager(-equivalent) support. The biggest downside is that it's a gnu project so nonfree software support will always be secondary, and IIRC there were still enough sharp edges when I tried it that I went back to Lix. But I wish them well and hope they succeed!

So I'd say either Lix (if you want to be able to interop with the broader Nix ecosystem) or Guix (if you like Scheme, copyleft, or a more cohesive system).

AFAIK none of snix/tvix/etc are usable as a replacement for the cppnix binary in the way Lix/Detsys Nix are.

I do like the channel determinate offers with the built-in dependency cooldown. I haven't checked recently to see if that's available from anywhere else

Lix because I trust the dev team more than any other Nix-like, with Guix as a close second in that regard. Not Guix because I don't like lisp and I do like the convenience of the world's largest package repository.

if you aren't sure, just use the primary implementation (nix / cppnix). it's the most well-supported, with the largest community around it, and the most nix developers and nix / nixos contributors working on it. the vast majority of people working on nixos use nix.

detnix is for detsys to move faster and do things specific to their clients' needs without being impeded by the development cadence of upstream nix, and to do things that upstream nix wouldn't accept for various reasons. there is effectively no reason to use this unless you're a client of detsys because the benefits don't really manifest without a support contract. they have a few cool things that won't be upstreamed, but you aren't going to find help in the main nix/nixos support channels using them, and they are arguably less battle-tested by nature of simply having fewer users that only do things on the happy path.

lix has a bunch of objectives, but at the present moment it's effectively upstream nix with some decent dreams (e.g., "demoting" flakes from core into a form of plugin system, and levelling the playing field for alternative implementations of similar ideas) and, in various areas, cleaned-up code. largely they haven't deviated far enough from upstream nix yet for it to matter from an end-user perspective, but right now there's no point locking in to using it if you're in a position where you're asking this question. the improvements between (cpp)nix and lix are cyclical, with a lot of them in one ending up in the other, because there is significant development overlap. it's also a bit more "community-focused", but said community is very small.

guix the implementation is an entirely different story. it's for guix the operating system, and has a bunch of different expectations entirely. the only similarity is that it uses some components of the nix store. a sibling comment mentions that it uses a "proper language" which is an implication i'd suggest isn't quite correct—nix is indeed a "proper language". "it uses a general-purpose language" would be more apt: nix the language is focused exclusively on package management, whereas guix uses a full scheme ( guile , specifically). if you're interested in nix/nixos, guix is not the thing for this. if you're interested in the guix ecosystem, guix is the only thing for this, but that comes with…

items.content_ko: 저자는 Determinate Nix, Lix, Guix 등을 비교한다. Determinate Nix는 기업 버전이며, 상류(upstream)에 개선 사항을 반영하지 않고 기능을 억지로 추가할 수 있다는 우려가 있다. Lix는 생태계의 불편한 점을 고치고 복잡한 코드베이스를 정리하려는 방향이며, 특별한 사용을 하지 않는 한 cppnix와 호환된다고 한다. Guix는 제대로 된 프로그래밍 언어를 쓰고 home-manager에 해당하는 기능을 일급으로 지원하지만, GNU 프로젝트라 비자유 소프트웨어 지원은 부차적이다. 저자는 Guix를 한 번 써 봤지만 불편한 부분이 있어 다시 Lix로 돌아갔다. 결론으로 Nix 생태계와의 상호운용을 원하면 Lix를, Scheme이나 카피레프트, 일관된 시스템을 원하면 Guix를 추천한다. Snix와 Tvix는 아직 쓸 만하지 않다는 내용이 이어지지만 본문은 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Proton users cancel subscriptions following CEO Andy Yen’s “loser thinking” remarks
items.content:
Proton users say they canceled subscriptions after 404 Media reported CEO Andy Yen pushed faster AI-assisted coding.

The report cites interviews with 8 current and 1 former employee, plus internal Slack chats and recordings.

Yen reportedly called delaying code for security testing “bullshit and loser thinking,” sparking user anger.

Some users have called for Yen to resign, arguing Proton risks losing its privacy-focused reputation.

Key Takeaways by nexos.ai , reviewed by Cybernews staff.

Users of Proton services report canceling their subscriptions following damning coverage by 404 Medi a, which suggests that the company’s CEO, Andy Yen, pushes AI use despite security concerns.

The exclusive report, based on interviews with 8 current and 1 former Proton employees and a review of Slack chats, meeting recordings, and the firm’s AI manifesto, resulted in a major PR crisis for the Swiss company behind ProtonMail and other privacy tools.

After an employee suggested taking at least a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live, Yen reportedly responded by calling the idea “bullshit and loser thinking,” saying it is possible to both be fast and secure.

Yen, a former CERN particle physicist, allegedly told the team to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more,” according to 404 Media.

OpenAI quadruples bug bounty rewards amid AI-enabled hacking fears

Proton issues an apology, says its AI use will never come at the expense of security

Think twice before asking AI to check your mole: new test shows surprising results

Exclusive: Political deepfakes target Democrats more than Republicans ahead of midterms

Nvidia CEO targeted by alleged Chinese spy

ChatGPT told laid-off Amazon engineer to stop taking life-saving drugs and lie to doctors

The publication sparked a backlash on Reddit, with users publicly announcing their departures from Proton tools.

One Redditor addressed Yen, saying he misses the “fundamental” reason many people choose Proton: the Swiss firm is the opposite of “a giant techbro company.”

We don’t want another Google or Microsoft; we want a company that shares our ideals, and Proton was that for many of us, at least in some sense. The customer decides if a product is quality, not the CEO,

Such comparisons may be especially harmful to Proton, which positions itself as a privacy-focused alternative to big tech companies and an advocate of European digital sovereignty.

Some users are calling for Yen to resign to save the company’s reputation. One Redditor said he canceled his subscription until the current CEO steps down.

Another Reddit user said it makes “no sense” for them to stay if Yen wants to double down on AI code generation and “eliminate all the checks and balances that maintain the quality of their codebase.”

There are also calls for Yen’s resignation on Proton’s user forum on the company’s website, where the post garnered 831 likes and dozens of comments at the time of writing.

Cybernews reached out to Proton for comment and will update the article once it receives a response.

404 Media reported that employees at the company feel unable to voice their concerns about developing AI-driven security products for fear of being berated by Yen or losing their jobs.

“The CEO is in full AI psychosis and has been for a while now,” an employee is cited as saying.

Earlier in October, 404 Media cited a leaked email saying that Proton was planning to interview employees to assess how they apply AI in their roles.

The company said that the interviews could have consequences for employees’ future at the company, including changes in roles and the continuation of employment.

While AI use was initially banned in the company, Proton reportedly recently installed software on employees’ computers to track how much code is AI-generated. In addition, the company reportedly plans to stop hiring human engineers and write more code with AI.

items.title: Thinking in Traits
items.content:
Rust favors composition over inheritance.

I’m sure you’ve heard that before, but rarely does anyone take the time to explain what it means in practice.

Also, why is this model the right choice for Rust?

Let’s take a step back and look at an example: have you ever asked yourself why collect() works the way it does?

let doubled : Vec <_> = numbers . iter () . map ( | x | x * 2 ) . collect ();

How does collect know to produce a Vec here?

To answer that, let’s first look at the signature of Iterator::collect :

fn collect < B : FromIterator < Self :: Item >>( self ) -> B

In fact, it doesn’t “know” about any collection type or any other type, for that matter.

The thing it does know is that whatever type you want must be capable of constructing itself from an iterator.

And Vec<_> happens to be a type that does.

Further note that we didn’t specify the element type of the vector.

The compiler is clever enough to infer that from the context!

The mechanism is the same for any other supported type, like hash maps, strings, or any custom collection type of your choosing as long as it implements FromIterator for the iterator’s item type.

And what “collecting” means is also defined by the type itself.

A String , for example, has the ability to collect characters:

let string : String = chars . iter () . collect (); // "abc"

And a HashMap can collect key-value pairs:

let pairs = [( "a" , 1 ), ( "b" , 2 ), ( "c" , 3 )];

let map : HashMap <_, _> = pairs . iter () . cloned () . collect ();

It’s only fair to mention that interfaces can also express shared contracts.

Here, two independently defined implementations connect through a shared item type.

This is “composition through contracts”:

Any of these iterators can feed into any of these collections as long as the bounds are satisfied. For example, HashSet<T> also requires T: Eq + Hash .

Here, a producer yields values of some type T through the Iterator trait.

On the other side, a collection implements FromIterator<T> to describe how it can build itself from those values.

The shared item type T connects the two contracts, and collect() is the bridge between them.

It requires only that the destination can be constructed from the items the iterator yields.

In our first example, the Vec<_> annotation selects the destination type.

Because Vec<T> implements FromIterator<T> , the compiler knows how to connect that destination to our iterator.

collect() is the glue that passes the iterator to that implementation, which creates and fills the vector.

Note how neither side needs to know the concrete type on the other side.

The iterator doesn’t need to know how a vector stores its elements.

And the vector doesn’t need to know where the items came from, only how to iterate over them.

That means we can extend either side independently.

A new iterator can feed existing collections, and a new collection implementing FromIterator<T> can accept existing iterators yielding T .

We don’t need a separate conversion for every producer–collection pair.

All we need is one implementation, and collect() is the glue that brings it all together.

In simple Rust pseudocode, we can expand the calls step by step:

while let Some (item) = iterator . next () {

The value of an abstraction is the code that no longer needs to exist between its users.

Class inheritance models “is-a” relationships.

In Java, for example, an SSLSocket is a subclass of Socket .

An encrypted socket is still a socket, after all.

But does every socket operation make sense for it?

Socket.shutdownOutput() lets a TCP connection stop sending while continuing to receive, a feature called “half-closing.”

Code using a socket might therefore do this:

void finishSending ( Socket socket) throws IOException {

On Android API levels 21 through 23, the platform’s SSLSocket implementations rejected this operation with UnsupportedOperationException .

items.summary_ko: Rust는 상속보다 조합(composition)을 선호한다는 원칙을 실제 예시로 설명한다. collect()는 특정 컬렉션 타입을 알지 못하고, 원하는 타입이 이터레이터로부터 자신을 만들 수 있는 FromIterator를 구현하고 있는지만 확인한다. 컴파일러는 문맥으로 요소 타입도 추론한다.
items.content_ko: 글은 let doubled: Vec<_> = numbers.iter().map(|x| x * 2).collect(); 코드를 예로 든다. collect의 시그니처는 B: FromIterator<Self::Item>을 요구하며, 이 함수는 어떤 컬렉션 타입도 직접 알지 못한다. 대신 반환 타입 B가 이터레이터로부터 생성될 수 있어야 한다는 조건만 안다. Vec<_>가 이 조건을 만족하며, 요소 타입은 명시하지 않아도 컴파일러가 문맥에서 추론한다. 같은 방식이 해시 맵, 문자열, 그리고 이터레이터의 아이템 타입에 대해 FromIterator를 구현한 임의의 커스텀 컬렉션에도 적용된다. 본문은 여기서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: 도청 당하는것같은데 어떡하죠 ㅠ
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

제가 집에서 한 말이나 제 언니랑 한 말들을 학교 가면 다 알고있어요 그래서 제가 말한 내용이랑 똑같은 내용을 꼭 제가 들을 수 있을때 언급하고 남자애들 여자애들 할것없이 제가 안보이는 데에서 조금만 이상한 말 하면 비웃으면서 지나가요 ㅠ 제가 진짜 친구가 없어서 학교에서 한마디도 안하는 날들이 대부분인데 제가 언니랑 학교 구석에서 말한 내용이랑 집에서 혼잣말 한 내용들을 똑같이 언급한게 한두번이 아니에요 ㅠ 제가 그냥 내용만 겹치면 말을 않겠는데 제가 말했던 내용 언급하면서 꼭 제 이름도 한번씩 부르고 그래요 보통 사람들은 자기이름을 그렇게 말하면 기분나빠서 한번 돌아보기라도 하겠지만 저는 성격이 워낙 내성적이라 누가 비웃고 지나가거나 째려보거나 저 보면서 한숨쉬어도 아무말도 못하거든요 ㅠ 그래서 그냥 기분만 나쁜건데 이게 하루이틀 쌓이니까 너무 힘들더라고요 ㅠ 처음엔 저도 이게 정신이 약간 아픈건가 했는데 정신병 관련 영상도 다 보고 그랬는데 환청은 이런식으로 들리는게 아니라고 하더라고요 계속 날 비난하고 그런식으로 들리는건데 저는 그런게 전혀 아니라 제가 전날 했던 얘기들, 방금 쉬는시간에 학교 구석에서 나눈 얘기들을 자꾸 똑같이 언급하니까 미치겠어요 ㅠ 한두번 우연으로 겹치는게 아니라 계속 겹쳐요 진짜.. 그리고 애초에 제가 학교에서 말을 한마디도 안하는데 자꾸 저한테 그런 반응을 보인다는게 애초에 저한테 이상한 일이 일어난다는 반증 아닌가요? 그리고 걔네가 말했던걸 몇개를 말씀드려보면 제가 도청을 의심한 초기에 급식실에서 밥먹고있었는데 어떤 남자애가 “도청” 이러고 지나가는거에요 그리고 저희반 남자애가 제 언니 이동수업반이랑 같은 반인데 거기서 쉬는시간에 “도청기를 달고다녀 ㅋㅋㅋㅋ” 이랬다는거에요 진짜 이상하죠 저는 예전에 우울증 약을 먹은적이 있어서 정신이 막 무결점으로 건강한 편은 아니에요 근데 저희 언니는 그런적도 없고 교우관계도 좋고 진짜 정신이 건강하거든요 ㅠ 근데 저희 언니가 그런말을 들었다니깐 진짜 도청이 일어나는게 맞는거구나 생각했어요.. 그리고 또 있었던 일을 말씀드리면 이동수업 때 제 뒷쪽에서 남자애가 제 아버지 직업을 언급하면서 제 이름을 말하는거에요 이게 도청을 하지 않고서는 절대 알수가 없는 사실이거든요 ㅠ 또 “정신병ㅋㅋㅋ” 하면서 제 이름을 언급하는거에요 이것도 도청을 하지 않았다면 알수 없는거고요 더 말씀드릴 사례가 많은데 그러면 너무 길어져서 이정도만 말씀드릴게요 그래서 찾아보니까 머리에 붙일수 있는 초소형 도청기가 있다길래  제 언니가 제 머리를 샅샅이 뒤져줬거든요? 근데 그래도 아무것도 안나오더라고요 ㅠ 그리고 또 도청 탐지 업체를 알아보니까 금액이 너무 비싸서요 ㅠ 제가 고3인데 이런일을 당해서 너무 스트레스 받는데 방법이 없어서 정말 어떻게 해야될지 모르겠어요 안그래도 제가 여자애들이나 남자애들이 괴롭힐 소재가 많은 조용한 애거든요 ㅠ그래서 저를 지나칠때 꼭 한마디 끼얹고 지나가고 그래서 학교생활이 막 편한 그런애는 아닌데 학교에서 유일하게 맘놓고 말할 수 있는 언니랑 말하는 얘기를 다 알고있으니까 스트레스 받아서 공부 능력도 점점 떨어지는것같고 쨋든 걱정이 이만저만이 아니에요 어떡해야되죠 ㅠㅠ 제가 성격이 활발한 편도 아니고 집에 돈이 많지도 않아서 진짜 대학 잘가야되는데 걱정이에요ㅠㅠ 긴글 읽어주셔서 감사하고요 여기가 사생활 침해 관련한 갤러리니까 혹여나 저랑 비슷한 경험이 있으시거나 관련 지식이 있는 분은 제가 어떻게 해야하는건지 알려주시면 진짜진짜 감사드릴것같아요 많은 도움 부탁드려요 정말 방법 여러가지 찾아봐도 안되겠어서 여기다 글 남겨요

items.title: If you love a website, back it up
items.content:
This story starts with a little tragedy. See, I’ve got these old webpages I love to go back and look on every now and then. There’s websites that have been online unchanged for years and years, or decades, and there’s something a little cozy about checking in on them every now and then to see an old friend is still doing okay. Sometimes, of course, tragedy strikes.

There was this fansite called teapuppies.com for an old anime series and and toy line called Ochaken . It’s about these cute cartoon dog characters who have tea leaves for ears, each of them named after a different kind of tea. 1 The site had been online since 2004 and had basically not changed since 2005, but it was nice just having it around. Except when I went to visit it a few weeks ago, and discovered that not only was the site gone but the domain is now being used to serve online gambling ads.

I work in web archiving, by the way. Which is to say that I should have known the site would go offline someday, and that I have the tools to have done something about it. I could have archived that site while it was still around, but I didn’t. This post is here to beg you to do what I didn’t think to, and to teach you how.

You see, when I talk to a lot of people about web archiving, they always seem to believe it’s something they couldn’t do. It’s something a big organization like the Internet Archive does, and if you want a webpage to be saved you just have to wait and hope it gets done. But that’s not true! What I really want everyone to know is that you have control over the world around you, you can take action to preserve things and make things better. And not just can , but should ! Don’t just wait for someone else to act - get out there and and make it happen! Got a favourite site? Back it up! Got some information you don’t want to get lost? Back it up! Favourite post somewhere? All together now. Back! It! Up!

All of the tools I’ll be showing off in this post use standard web archiving formats like WARC 2 . You don’t have to worry about any of the technical details 3 , but I’m telling you that because it means there are a lot of really great tools to do whatever you want with them. Here, just as an example, is an entire archived website embedded right in this blog post:

You can even click through all the links, look at all of the images, the works. It’s an entire website right in a post! (And if you don’t trust me to keep this up, and you want the web archive to host somewhere else? You can download it for yourself right from there. Just click the kebab menu and choose “download archive”, and you can do whatever you like with it. In fact, please do!)

By the way, for disclosure: the tools I’m going to mention in this blog post are made by the company I work for, but that’s not because they’ll pay my salary (most of them are free!). I just happen to think these are the best tools there are for personal web archiving.

Option 1 - ArchiveWeb.page browser extension

By far the easiest personal web archiving tool is the ArchiveWeb.page browser extension for Chrome. This doesn’t take much in the way of setup or technical skills, and it works for anything: a single page, an entire website, a social media post or profile. So long as you can see it in a web browser, you can save it. All you really need to do is:

Visit the first page you want to archive.

Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click “Start Archiving”.

If your page has any interactive elements, click on those to make sure all their data loads.

Visit any other pages you want captured in the same collection and let the extension grab them.

Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click “Stop Archiving”.

items.title_ko: 오래된 웹사이트를 좋아한다면 백업해 두세요
items.summary_ko: 웹 아카이빙 업무를 하는 필자는 오랫동안 즐겨 찾던 팬사이트 teapuppies.com이 사라지고 도메인이 온라인 도박 광고를 송출하는 데 쓰이는 것을 확인했다. 필자는 사이트가 살아 있을 때 아카이빙하지 않은 것을 후회하며, 독자들에게 좋아하는 웹사이트를 미리 백업하라고 권한다. 글은 그 방법도 함께 설명하겠다고 말한다.
items.content_ko: 필자는 옛 웹페이지를 가끔 찾아보는 습관이 있다고 밝힌다. 애니메이션과 장난감 라인 Ochaken의 팬사이트 teapuppies.com은 차 잎을 귀처럼 단 강아지 캐릭터들을 다뤘고, 캐릭터마다 다른 차 이름이 붙어 있었다. 이 사이트는 2004년부터 온라인에 있었고 2005년 이후 거의 바뀌지 않았다. 그런데 몇 주 전 방문했을 때 사이트는 사라졌고, 도메인은 온라인 도박 광고를 보여주고 있었다. 필자는 웹 아카이빙 분야에서 일하고 있어 사이트가 언젠가 사라질 수 있다는 것과 이를 보존할 도구가 있다는 것을 알았지만, 사이트가 살아 있을 때 아카이빙하지 않았다고 고백한다. 이 글은 독자들이 필자처럼 뒤늦게 후회하지 않도록 미리 백업하라고 권하고, 그 방법을 알려주기 위해 쓰였다.

items.title: Stop Hardcoding Your Timeouts
items.content:
A developer rant about tools built for one kind of internet

Recently, I’ve been losing my mind to hardcoded timeouts . Silent, arbitrary, unconfigurable time limits baked into tools by developers who apparently have never had to wait more than 200ms for anything in their lives.

Now that coding agents are everywhere, everyone is using skills. The popular way to add them is through packages developed by vercel-labs, and the go-to collection is awesome-copilot , a curated set of skills sitting at 30K+ stars at the time of writing. Except I can’t use it. The repository is too big, and the npx skills installer just chokes and dies.

There’s an open issue about this since February #278 on the vercel-labs/skills repo and no one has responded. I’d be happy to send a PR and fix it myself. I just need someone to acknowledge it exists.

Is there a configuration option? A --timeout flag? An environment variable? No, there is nothing.

The workaround I found? Clone the repo manually first, then install from the local copy. It works, mostly. Except now skills-lock.json points to a path on my machine. My colleagues cannot use it. I also have to update my copy everytime I want update my skills. One workaround creates a lot of other problems.

Then came Docker Gordon, the AI-powered debugging assistant baked into Docker. Useful concept. I was stepping through a container build issue, the kind that requires iteration: tweak, rebuild, inspect, repeat. I’ve never used Gordon but when the error manifested itself, it came with a suggestion to try Gordon and so I did.

Except Gordon has a hard limit: if your container doesn’t finish building within two minutes , it gives up. The session dies. You start over.

A two-minute build might sound like plenty if you’re in a fast environment with warm caches and pulled base images. But if you’re pulling a fresh base image over a slower connection? Debugging a multi-stage build with several heavy layers? Forget it. Gordon has already moved on.

There is no way to configure this. No GORDON_TIMEOUT=600 env var. No --build-timeout flag. Nothing. The tool just assumes that two minutes is forever, and if you need more, that’s your problem.

Developers often working on fast machines, in offices or homes with gigabit connections, in cities with world-class infrastructure. They build tools with timeout defaults that reflect their own experience. And then they ship those tools to the whole world, with no knobs to turn.

The thing is, timeouts need to exist. Infinite waits are bad. Hanging processes are bad. I’m not arguing against timeouts. I’m arguing against unconfigurable timeouts. Against the implicit message that says: if you can’t do this in 60 seconds, your environment is wrong, not my assumption.

This isn’t hard. It’s respect for your users.

I’m writing this from Cairo. My internet is decent, better than many places in the world. But it’s not 1 Gbps symmetric fiber. It’s not co-located next to an npm registry mirror. A git clone of a large repo takes time. Pulling a Docker image takes time. These are not failures. They are physics.

When your tool dies silently after 60 seconds without any way to change that limit, you haven’t built a tool for the world. You’ve built a tool for your office.

And this matters more than most developers acknowledge. The global developer community isn’t located in San Francisco or Amsterdam or London. It’s in Lagos, in Karachi, in Cairo. It’s people on 4G connections, on shared broadband, on connections that have real latency because the nearest CDN edge is 50ms away instead of 5.

When you assume a fast connection, you’re not making a neutral technical decision. You’re making a statement about whose experience matters.

I don’t think anyone is doing this maliciously. I think it’s a blind spot. Your internet is fast, so a 60-second timeout feels generous. Your machines are powerful, so a 2-minute build window seems like plenty.

But please: before you ship a timeout, ask…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Handling Your First GHSA: A Guide for Open Source Maintainers
items.content:
This year, for the first time, the CVE program will publish around 100,000 vulnerabilities in a single year . CVE.ICU counts 88,601 through 29 October, up 125.3% on the same date in 2025. A large share of them land on open source projects, where the people triaging the report, writing the fix and shipping the release are mostly unpaid volunteers managing this wave on top of everything else.

For many of those records, and for most projects hosted on GitHub, it starts the same way for the maintainer on the other end: a private report in the Security tab. It arrives quietly, with no public trace, to whoever administers the repository, and in most projects that is one person. There is no template, and every tutorial you find explains how to request a CVE without saying what to do first. Most maintainers meet that moment alone, on their first advisory, with the reporter waiting. That is the moment The Maintainer’s Guide to GitHub Security Advisories is written for. Its first release is v2026-10 , and this post is a tour of what is inside and why.

In the projects we help under the OpenJS Foundation CNA , the fix is rarely where a first-timer gets stuck. The code change is usually small. What stalls people is the uncertainty around it, what comes next, what goes first, how things will land, while you are reacting to a security report for the first time and feeling the pressure.

Is this report even mine? Nobody checks a submission before it reaches you. In Lodash, around 95% of the reports we receive get closed , many with a proof of concept that runs. You decide scope, not the reporter, and saying no is a normal outcome , as long as you say why ( §4 ).

Your CI does not run. In the temporary private fork where you build the fix, status checks do not run , and in practice neither do Actions ( Limitations ). Whatever you normally trust a pipeline to catch, you are now catching by hand, in whichever environments you can recreate yourself ( §5 ).

The merge squashes everything. All the advisory’s pull requests merge at once, each landing on its branch as a single commit titled “Merge commit from fork” ( real example ). If you rely on conventional commits or a changelog generator, you will be amending and force-pushing before you tag, and that is expected, not a mistake ( Limitations ).

Publishing deletes the fork. When you publish the advisory, GitHub deletes the temporary private fork where you built the fix, with every review comment, every branch and every alternative you discussed and discarded. The confirmation dialog says so, and it is the last thing you read before the button ( Limitations ).

Each of those has a wrong answer that costs real time, and you usually meet them with the clock already running.

We kept answering the same questions. Running the OpenJS CNA , which went from three CVEs last year to almost 150 so far this year , we onboarded project after project and had the same conversation in each one, usually in a private thread, usually with a reporter waiting, and usually a week or two before the maintainer hit the exact problem we had just explained somewhere else. With report volume where it is and report quality all over the place, we could not keep teaching the process one advisory at a time. So we wrote it once, ahead of the next question.

The content is the security structure we built for Express in 2024 and brought to Lodash in 2025, with the project names removed: shared triage instead of one person, a written threat model, a CNA for CVEs, GitHub advisories as the channel, and an incident response plan that documents the security release. It is opinionated, it is based on firsthand experience, and the screenshots come from real advisories we handled.

items.summary_ko: CVE 프로그램은 올해 처음으로 약 10만 건의 취약점을 공개할 것으로 보인다. 많은 취약점이 오픈소스 프로젝트에 집중되며, 그 대부분은 자원봉사자가 관리한다. 글은 GitHub 보안 권고(GHSA)를 처음 다루는 메인테이너를 위한 안내서 『The Maintainer's Guide to GitHub Security Advisories』의 첫 릴리스 v2026-10을 소개한다.
items.content_ko: CVE.ICU 집계에 따르면 10월 29일까지 88,601건이 공개되었으며, 이는 2025년 같은 날짜보다 125.3% 많은 수치다. 많은 취약점이 오픈소스 프로젝트에 해당하며, 보고서 분류·수정·릴리스를 담당하는 사람들은 대부분 무급 자원봉사자다. GitHub에 호스팅된 대부분의 프로젝트에서는 보안 탭을 통한 비공개 보고로 시작되며, 보통 저장소 관리자 한 사람이 이를 받게 된다. 대부분의 튜토리얼은 CVE를 요청하는 방법만 설명하고 그 전에 무엇을 해야 하는지는 말하지 않는다. 이 안내서는 그 순간을 위해 쓰였다. OpenJS Foundation CNA에 속한 프로젝트들에서는 처음 하는 사람이 수정 자체보다는 다른 부분에서 막히는 경우가 많으며, 코드 변경은 보통 작다고 한다. 본문은 여기서 끊겨 있다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

items.title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks
items.content:
Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432

No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating.

Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432 , a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update.

Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables.

Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.

items.content_ko: Ubuntu LTS 커널에 대해 치명적 취약점 CVE-2026-98432의 패치가 아직 나오지 않았다. 이 취약점은 CVSS 9.8로 평가되며, 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 LTS 릴리스 모두 벤더 업데이트 없이 남아 있다. 따라서 해당 릴리스를 운영하는 관리자는 취약점을 막아 주는 공식 커널 패키지가 없는 상태다. 특히 인터넷에 노출되어 있거나 격리를 위해 Ubuntu LTS 커널의 권한 경계에 의존하는 멀티테넌트 자가 호스팅 시스템에서 위험이 크다. 패키지가 나오기 전까지 이 호스트들은 CVE가 허용하는 원격 또는 로컬 공격에 계속 노출된다. Ubuntu는 수정 예정일을 발표하지 않았으며, 관리자들은 기본 커널을 유지할지, 외부 완화 조치가 있다면 적용할지, 패치가 적용된 릴리스나 커널로 워크로드를 옮길지 판단해야 한다.

items.title: My favourite laptop
items.content:
I’m not a big owner of things, but the best laptop I’ve ever owned is a roughed-up

For the flex, here it is running a GUI shell sat on top of the microkernel I’m currently

working on (blog post about this incoming… eventually).

Here’s a list of things that I think make it brilliant. I don’t want to pretend that any

of these things are uniquely exemplary: far from it. It is the confluence of them, and

not any one in particular, that makes me love using it.

It’s pretty tiny. Its form-factor fits snuggly into the footprint of an A4 piece of

paper, so it sits alongside books and folders when placed in a small rucksack without

It weighs almost nothing too: even with the extra capacity battery, it’s only about 1.45

Kg. Light enough that you almost don’t notice it when travelling.

Mine has an i5-5200U: 4 logical cores, maxing out at 2.7 GHz. I upgraded it to 8 GB of

RAM a while back: more than enough for some light on-the-go programming.

Even at full pelt, I’ve never heard the fan kicking up much of a fuss. Now that I think

about it, I’m not even certain that it works.

The X250 has both an internal battery and an external battery slot. I’ve opted for the

largest after-market external battery I could find. When doing casual work the laptop

will easily survive for north of 10 hours without a charge, stretching to 12 hours if

The X250 was quite popular and replacement parts retail very cheaply on ebay. It’s not

the easiest to disassemble Thinkpad by any means but I can tear it apart entirely with

the pocket phillips I keep on my keyring. I have previously replaced:

Every time you open up a laptop you run the risk of damaging something important either

via a slip of the hand or simply the accumulated toll of loosening and tightening dozens

of tiny screw threads. Despite that, my X250 has proved remarkably resilient and has

never sustained any major damage despite more than more than a dozen tear-downs.

As with most Thinkpads, the keyboard feels lovely to use. When you spend a lot of time

writing code the reliability and sensitivity of a keyboard starts to matter a lot.

Coupled with my text editor , the experience of writing code on the thing

I opted for Endeavour OS. In the usual Arch Linux tradition, it favours native

package installs over sandboxed applications. As a result my install sits at around 30

GB. A 128 GB M.2 SSD raided from another second-hand machine is more than enough to

cover that and everything I’m working on.

I’ve slimmed down my systemd setup as much as possible and the thing boots from cold in

Here’s where the X250 beats out most competition. I bought mine second-hand for about

£100 in 2018. They’ve only got cheaper since then. I’m not afraid to take it anywhere

because it’s barely worth stealing and would be cheap to replace even if that were to

happen. Its value is very much not in its on-paper specs and instead in how I use it.

I get a certain glee in keeping older or second-hand hardware running as a daily driver.

It sounds silly, but it feels like a quiet revolt against bigger-faster-costlier

consumption culture. Come the end times, this is the machine I’ll be riding it out with.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
items.content:
One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet

Google says a manufacturer ‘intentionally’ hijacked its devices with malware.

Google says a manufacturer ‘intentionally’ hijacked its devices with malware.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A current Videostrong Android TV device. Image: Videostrong

Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and “cut ties” with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them.

The infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for “malicious activity,” like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the “backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain,” saying:

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army

It wasn’t just one device that was impacted, either — the malware was found “built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years.” Most of those were Android TV set-top boxes, but the botnet also infected other “Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.”

Google says Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to load the malware onto users’ devices after they booted up the hardware for the first time. Google also says it made changes to its review process for device manufacturers after this incident.

items.title: Maintainer spotlight: Anthony Bolden (@Walnut356) | Inside Rust Blog
items.content:
There are hundreds of people who maintain the Rust toolchain, often on a volunteer basis on top of another job. The Rust Content team is working on a series of blog posts highlighting some of these prolific contributors to recognize the awesome work that they are doing in order to make Rust better for everyone. You can find the previous post here .

Consider donating to the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund if you'd like to support Rust Project maintainers.

In this post, we would like to introduce Anthony Bolden ( @Walnut356 ). Anthony is a self-taught programmer who went on a mission to improve the Rust debugger experience. This year, he participated as a contributor in the Google Summer of Code program, and recently he joined the Rust compiler team.

We interviewed Anthony to find out what brought him to programming and how he became an expert on debuggers. Read more below!

Can you briefly introduce yourself and tell us how you started with programming?

Hello, my name is Anthony Bolden, also known as @Walnut356 , and I live in Wisconsin. I do not have any formal computer science education and I've never had a job in the tech industry, so my journey to programming was a bit different. I work overnight shifts in a hotel, where I often have a lot of time to spare, and I needed something to occupy my mind. For I while, I used to solve puzzles or read books, but eventually I got tired of that.

I wanted to find a long-term project, so I tried programming. It took me a couple of tries until it "clicked", but when that happened, I instantly fell in love with it. It is so much fun!

I bought a couple of C++ books when I was learning how to program, so that was my entrypoint. But I was very dissatisfied with the development experience there. I wanted to make a simple game, because I've always found game design fascinating, but adding a dependency like SDL to my project turned out to be very difficult. I spent SO MUCH time trying to get it to work, and it didn't help that I was doing it on Windows. It should not be that hard!

I really enjoy low-level programming, optimization work, reading assembly for fun… but C++ was not for me. So I switched to Python, even though I was not super satisfied with its performance and its typical use-cases. At the time, I played Super Smash Bros. Melee competitively, and I wanted to analyze replays from my matches to improve my play. There was an existing Python replay parser, but it was outdated and slow. I forked it, and through painstaking effort I managed to double its performance. But when working with thousands of replays and gigabytes of data, it still took an hour to process everything in Python.

Then I realized that the original author of the Python parser abandoned it because they ran into the same performance problems. They decided to rewrite it in Rust instead. I took a look at the Rust code, but it seemed really complicated. It took me a few tries to break through the syntax barrier, but it didn't take long to realize that Rust is exactly where I wanted to be. It gave me the power to express exactly what I wanted, it was incredibly fast, and I didn't have to constantly fight just to add a dependency or build my project.

You are doing a lot of work in the area of debuggers. What started that interest?

When I started with Rust, I solved a lot of Advent of Code tasks, and I was debugging constantly , because it was my first exposure to data structures and algorithms.

One day, CodeLLDB, which is a Visual Studio Code debugger plugin that I was using, removed their built-in Rust support, instead falling back to the visualizer scripts Rust distributes in its toolchains. That instantly made my debugging experience terrible, because those scripts weren't part of MSVC toolchains, and there were no alternatives at the time that would enable debugging with LLDB on Windows.

items.title: 글 쌌다 지웠다 하는 뷩쉰은 봐라
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.title: null ctf 풀이 하신분들?

해킹 문제를 해결하는 Capture The Flag(CTF)을 다루는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

오디오 파일로 변환해서 켜면 키보드 치는소리나오는거 까지만 하고 더이상 진행이 안되서 접었는데 풀이하신분 있으신가요?

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: US boy names that became girl names and vice versa
items.content:
Picture a baby named Leslie , Kelly , or Ashley , and you’ll probably picture a girl. But all three names were once given mostly to boys. Looking at US baby names from 1936 to 2025, we found that 42 shifted from mostly boys to mostly girls, while just 12 went the other way. Explore the charts below to see how each name changed and what drove the shifts in each direction.

125 names that moved between boys and girls

The chart below follows 125 names whose use among boys and girls has changed noticeably over time. Of those, 54 meet our stricter definition of a switch from one sex to the other.

Each row is a name, and each tile represents a five-year period, running from 1936 on the left to 2025 on the right. The color shows what percentage of babies given each name were girls, while gray tiles mark periods with too few recorded births for a reliable comparison. Select any name to explore its history on the interactive see-saw chart below.

The names are grouped by how they’ve changed. Some, like Aubrey and Lindsey , shifted from mostly boys to mostly girls and stayed there, while others, like Jean and Ollie , moved in the opposite direction.

Not every name made a complete switch. Charlie and Blake were once given mostly to boys but have become unisex, with a much more even split today, while names like Jamie and Robin have changed direction along the way.

Most names moved toward girls, and girls drove the change both ways

The most common shift was from boys to girls. Using a consistent definition of what qualifies as a switch, we found that 42 names moved from mostly boys to mostly girls, compared with just 12 that moved from mostly girls to mostly boys.

But the more interesting finding is what drove these changes. Think of each name as a see-saw, with boys on one end and girls on the other. A name can tip toward girls in two ways: more girls start getting it, or fewer boys do.

For each name that switched, we compared how often it was given to boys and girls before and after the shift. Of the 42 names that moved toward girls, 34 were driven mainly by an increase among girls , rather than a decline among boys.

Surprisingly, the same pattern held in the opposite direction. Of the 12 names that moved toward boys, 9 shifted mainly because fewer girls were receiving them , rather than because more boys were. In other words, whichever way a name moved, the biggest change usually came from girls.
