items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: A Raspberry Pi Just Got 26% Pricier. You Should Be Worried
items.content:
The beloved Raspberry Pi small-scale was never meant to cost this much. But after multiple price hikes, including an $80 increase announced today, the 16GB RAM model of the Raspberry Pi 5 now costs $385. If you’re hungry for some depressing RAM-driven sticker shock, that’s more than triple the $120 this same configuration cost when it launched in January 2025. Is this the worst timeline? It’s certainly not the best.

CEO Eben Upton blamed “a lack of alternative supply for 16GB DRAM, compounded by other ongoing component shortages” for the latest price hike in a blog post published Monday . Alongside the $80 price increase for the Raspberry Pi, the SBC (single-board computer) maker added that it will raise the cost of 16GB Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 variants by $40. Upton said the company would hold steady on other 16GB systems such as its Raspberry Pi 500+ keyboard computer.

Upton, who has had to write too many of these price-hike blog posts in the last year, called the latest decision “unavoidable.” To understand why, you have to look at the kinds of deals the major memory makers have been drafting lately. There are three major producers of DRAM, or dynamic random access memory: Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix. In its last few quarterly earnings reports, Micron has talked up multiyear contracts it has inked with major tech brands. And there is no relief to be found among the competition. Nascent Chinese memory makers, including CXMT , have strayed from making deals with the largest gadget brands, including Apple . Instead, they are focused on producing high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, to fuel China’s AI buildout, despite reportedly low manufacturing yields.

What’s most depressing about this Raspberry Pi news, then, is that it’s a stark reminder that memory prices are unlikely to improve next year. Moreover, the obscene price of memory, combined with the “cartel”-like activities of memory manufacturers, will affect smaller players more than it will major gadget companies. This is especially problematic for companies like Raspberry Pi that have historically prized affordability and customizability above all else.

The ongoing memory pricing crisis, often referred to as “RAMageddon,” is being driven by the push to produce HBM for AI hyperscalers, which is inundating small towns throughout the United States. This demand for consumer-end memory has driven up the prices of practically every gadget from the largest tech manufacturers. But in the end, the smallest companies are the casualties of ruined memory supply chains. Multiple heads of smaller gadget companies have told me that the price of mere megabytes of memory has increased by a factor of six.

Upton reiterated, in his post, that the memory crunch is “only temporary.” But with ongoing memory contracts controlling the largest conglomerates’ prices, it doesn’t seem that smaller brands have much power to negotiate. Just last week, SK Hynix said in its latest quarterly earnings report that RAM demand will outstrip supply through to 2030. That memory maker’s long-term agreements have already covered more than half of its planned production from 2027 into 2028. While these semiconductor companies make bank, the little guy—along with his loyal consumers—gets screwed over the most.

items.title: All You Need Is Attention (Human, That Is)
items.content:
The paper that started all of this is called “Attention Is All You Need.” That’s the 2017 Google paper that gave us the transformer, which gave us GPT, which gave us Claude Code, which gave us the glorious mess I’m about to confess to.

And the joke that keeps rattling around in my head is this: the thing that makes the models work is attention . And the thing I’m fresh out of is attention . Mine. The human kind.

Here’s where my head is at. For a stretch there I had six, sometimes eight agents going at once. Different projects, spread across virtual desktops like a cockpit. One desktop grinding on a Go refactor. One writing tests. One spiking a feature I’d been putting off for a month. One answering a question about a codebase I hadn’t opened in a year.

It felt amazing . It felt like I’d finally cracked it. Look at me go.

And then I’d flip to desktop 3 and the agent had been sitting there for four hours waiting on me to answer a question. So I’d read half the question, say “yeah do that,” and flip to desktop 5. Which was also waiting. Repeat for an hour. I ended those sessions more tired than a day of actual coding, and I couldn’t tell you with a straight face what any of the eight agents had actually done .

That’s the tell. I wasn’t in flow. I was a human message broker between eight processes, and I was dropping packets.

Here’s the part that bothers me. When you overload yourself, you don’t stop reading everything at once. You keep your eyes moving over the words. What you quietly stop doing is understanding them. Reading and understanding are two different verbs, and under load I was doing the first and skipping the second — across the board.

And here’s the uncomfortable bit: the thing I skimmed hardest was the stuff I’d told myself was safe.

I’ve said before that tests are the real spec , and I still believe it. But watch what that belief turns into when you’re tired: “tests are the spec” quietly becomes “I glanced at the green checkmark.” Those are not the same thing. A passing suite I didn’t actually read is not verification — it’s a little green light I decided to trust. The gap between the tests passed and I understand what the tests prove is exactly where an agent gets away with murder.

So let me talk about the two places skimming bites you: the prose, and the design-and-tests.

The prose is the plan the agent writes before it starts, the “here’s what I changed and why” at the end, the PR description, the commit message, the paragraph where it lays out its reasoning . It’s the one place the agent tells you what it thinks it’s doing, as opposed to what it actually did.

Skimming it gets you the words. Understanding it gets you two things, and the second one is the one that matters:

That second one is the whole game, and it’s invisible to a skim. An agent that “cleaned up the function” and cheerfully lists six things it tidied, but never once mentions the retry semantics it quietly rewrote, is telling you something by omission . The dangerous change is almost never the one it brags about. It’s the one that didn’t make the summary. You only catch that if you’re reading for the gap — asking “what would I expect to see here that isn’t here?” — instead of nodding along to the parts that are present and well-written.

And AI prose is very well-written. That’s the trap. It reads confident and complete, so your brain files it as confident and complete and moves on. The absence doesn’t announce itself. You have to go looking.

I’m not the only one circling this. There’s a line from a talk at the AI Engineer conference that’s been quoted a bunch and it nails it: “code got cheap, attention didn’t.” That’s the whole ballgame right there. We 10x’d the production of code and the production of plausible-sounding English about code , and we did exactly nothing to increase the number of hours a human can actually pay attention in a day.

items.content_ko: 원문 본문이 중간에 끊겨 있다. 확인되는 내용은 다음과 같다. 글은 2017년 Google 논문 'Attention Is All You Need'에서 트랜스포머가 나왔고, 이것이 GPT와 Claude Code로 이어졌다는 말로 시작한다. 글쓴이는 한동안 6~8개의 에이전트를 여러 가상 데스크톱에 나눠 동시에 돌렸다. 프로젝트별로 Go 리팩터링, 테스트 작성, 미뤄 둔 기능 실험, 오래 열지 않은 코드베이스 질문 등을 맡겼다. 처음에는 대단하다고 느꼈지만, 한 데스크톱의 에이전트가 4시간 동안 답을 기다리고 있는 일이 생겼다. 그래서 질문을 대충 읽고 '그렇게 해'라고 답한 뒤 다음 데스크톱으로 넘기는 일이 반복됐고, 그 결과 실제 코딩을 하루 한 것보다 더 지쳤다고 한다.

items.title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
items.content:
Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts .

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings , extensive use of financial engineering , and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.

That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.

The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.

Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer.

Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.

The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.

Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense : they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.

Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts , Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments.

Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic.

First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies , including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses . Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%).

items.title: Hackers claim to have stolen 23TB of data from Russian statistics body, including Ukraine war casualty figures — Russian Federal State Statistics Service admits its servers were hit by cyberattacks.
items.content:
(Image credit: Belarusian CyberPartisans )

The Russian Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) admitted that its servers were hit by coordinated cyberattacks between October 29 and 31. However, it denied claims that tens of terabytes of data had been leaked, as asserted by hack groups like the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow. Rosstat stopped publishing annual cause-of-death statistics in 2024, but the hackers say that the huge new 23TB data haul includes data on Russian wartime losses marked “for official use only,” reports The Moscow Times . A new chart shared by the hack groups using the data suggests that as many as 50,000 Russian soldiers are killed every month.

Rosstat is very much like the U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics in the United States, or the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in the UK. It isn’t a big juicy military infrastructure target, but if accurate war casualty figures can come from the claimed exfiltrated data haul, then it would be a considerable win for Ukraine and its supporters.

Today @cpartisans and SilentCrow took down Russia's Federal State Statistics Service — the nerve center behind every socioeconomic number this regime produces.

Full breakdown below 👇 https://t.co/wUKfyUi6y6 November 1, 2026

As we mentioned in the intro, both the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow claim to have snagged lots of sensitive data from the Russian government thanks to this breach. The former’s tweet includes evidence and a breakdown. “Entire IT infrastructure wiped: Domain controllers, databases, servers, virtualization, document workflow, workstations, admin consoles, VPN,” notes a follow-up post about the Rosstat hack attack. “Systems destroyed: STATEK, CSOD, Demography, SED, ESSO, OFSN, internal employee surveillance, StatRegister, websites and more.”

This is a developing story with the Belarusian CyberPartisans promising to share more sensitive information from Rosstat after they have picked through it. The Rosstat website was reportedly defaced with hacker messages and logos. Rosstat remains inaccessible at the time of writing.

(Image credit: Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow) We spotted an interesting graphic shared by the Belarusian CyberPartisans , which included the Silent Crow logo. A chart indicates that over the last two years, between 25,000 and 50,000 Russian soldiers were killed every month. The October 2026 figure is just a smidgen under 50,000, if this data leak news is genuine.

These same hacking groups have claimed responsibility for the likes of the disruptive Aeroflot IT systems hack, and a state real estate company hack with two billion records, both in 2025. “Both groups are designated as extremist and banned in Russia,” notes the report.

items.summary_ko: 러시아 연방통계청(Rosstat)은 10월 29일부터 31일 사이 서버가 조직적인 사이버 공격을 받았다고 인정했지만, 수십 테라바이트의 데이터가 유출되었다는 주장은 부인했다. Belarusian CyberPartisans와 Silent Crow는 '공무용 전용(for official use only)'으로 표시된 전쟁 손실 자료를 포함한 23TB 규모의 데이터를 확보했다고 주장한다. 해커 측이 공유한 차트는 매달 최대 5만 명의 러시아 병사가 사망한다는 수치를 보여주지만, 이는 검증되지 않은 주장이다.
items.content_ko: Rosstat은 2024년 이후 사망 원인 통계 발표를 중단했다. 해커들은 이번에 확보한 데이터에 '공무용 전용'으로 표시된 전쟁 손실 자료가 들어 있다고 주장하고 있다. 보도는 The Moscow Times가 전했다. 기사는 Rosstat이 미국 Census Bureau, 노동통계국(BLS), 영국 ONS와 비슷한 통계 기관이며 군사 인프라 표적이 아니라고 설명한다. 필자는 유출 데이터에서 정확한 전쟁 사상자 수치가 나온다면 우크라이나와 그 지지국에 큰 성과가 될 것이라고 덧붙였다. 다만 이는 가정이며, 입력 내용에 데이터의 진위를 확인한 결과는 없다.

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Intel Stock Is Cratering After Trump Poured Taxpayer Money Into the Chipmaker: Did the Trump administration get some bad Intel?
items.content:
In August 2025, the Trump administration raised eyebrows by making a $8.9 billion investment in US chipmaker Intel, as part of a massive $100 billion drive to boost semiconductor supplies.

At first, it looked like an excellent investment as the AI race heated up as Intel saw shares shoot up, reaching just over $92 a share by Thursday of last week, more than quadrupling the government’s initial investment, as Yahoo Finance reports .

But by Friday, the situation looked dramatically different. Intel experienced its worst one-day stock performance since 1974, with shares cratering almost 30 percent on Friday alone. According to Yahoo , that means the value of the government’s 9.9 percent equity stake crashed from almost $40 billion to well under $30 billion, slicing over $11 billion in taxpayer-funded investment off its stake.

Intel’s shares are currently hovering at just over $60, well short of the “NOW $95” displayed in an AI slop image president Donald Trump shared of himself as a day trader in September.

The dramatic swing perfectly encapsulated why the government taking a major stake in a publicly traded company could result in investors being taken on a rollercoaster ride as the value of the Trump administration’s portfolio swings wildly.

Intel’s bruising Friday came after its shares had risen some 150 percent since the beginning of the year, cashing in on the seemingly limitless appetite for AI investments. But the company’s reported Q4 revenue outlook fell short of Wall Street expectations, triggering the major $150 billion market value wipeout.

Nonetheless, the chipmaker still managed to beat expectations in its third-quarter earnings report. The big elephant in the room was the personal computing industry, which has largely collapsed thanks to AI causing prices to skyrocket, suppressing consumer demand. Compounding its PC market woes are supply side production problems, as CNBC points out .

Investors are now divided on whether it’s time to buy the dip or wait it out as the stock swings drag on. Intel isn’t alone in feeling the hurt, with Google parent company Alphabet incurring massive losses and wiping out over half a trillion dollars in market value last week.

Zooming out, Big Tech is navigating a major point of reckoning as investors continue to ask hard questions about its ability to keep the party going and sustain its massive data center investments.

With existing supply woes, Intel is trapped between a rock and a hard place: either pursue a declining PC sector or make a major pivot to data center-friendly server processors, neither of which are a guarantee of future success.

Meanwhile, US taxpayers are along for the ride as the value of the Trump administration’s major investments in Intel continue to fluctuate wildly.

items.summary_ko: 2025년 8월 트럼프 행정부는 인텔에 89억 달러를 투자했다. 인텔 주가는 AI 열풍에 지난주 목요일 92달러 선을 넘어 정부의 초기 투자액보다 4배 이상 올랐지만, 금요일 하루에 30% 가까이 급락해 1974년 이후 최악의 하루 성과를 기록했다. 이에 따라 정부의 9.9% 지분 가치는 약 400억 달러에서 300억 달러 아래로 떨어졌다.
items.content_ko: 기사는 2025년 8월 트럼프 행정부가 미국 반도체 공급 확대를 위한 1000억 달러 규모 추진의 일환으로 인텔에 89억 달러를 투자한 사실을 짚는다. 초기에는 AI 경쟁이 달아오르며 인텔 주가가 치솟아 지난주 목요일 92달러 선을 넘었고, 이는 정부 초기 투자액의 4배 이상이었다. 그러나 금요일에는 주가가 거의 30% 폭락해 1974년 이후 가장 나쁜 하루 성과를 냈다. 이에 따라 정부가 보유한 9.9% 지분 가치는 약 400억 달러에서 300억 달러 아래로 떨어져 110억 달러 이상 줄었다. 인텔 주가는 현재 60달러대 초반에 머물고 있다. 기사는 상장 기업에 대한 정부 지분 투자가 투자자들에게 롤러코스터 같은 변동성을 가져올 수 있다고 지적하며, 트럼프 대통령이 9월 자신을 데이 트레이더로 묘사해 공유한 AI 생성 이미지의 'NOW $95' 문구를 언급한다. 본문은 중간에서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: An outsider's perspective on Scion and Mononoke
items.content:
An outsider’s perspective on Scion and Mononoke

Recently, Anthropic wrote a blog post about their new centralized version control system Scion . As someone working on the Source Control team at Databricks, where we have a huge monorepo and are exploring different options, I figured it might be useful to share my perspective here.

(Obligatory disclaimer: This post represents my own views, not my employer’s.)

I recommend reading Anthropic’s post before continuing to read this one.

You may also want to pre-read Rain Paharia’s Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke and the follow-up More on Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke .

Before we get into the weeds, it might be helpful to you to know where I’m coming from.

If you’re not interested in this, you can jump to the Technical Commentary section.

I have never worked at Facebook, but one of my all-time favorite tech talks is Durham Goode’s Scaling Mercurial at Facebook from Git Merge 2017. Goode was the longest-serving and most senior member on Facebook’s Source Control team. ( source )

The talk covers various interesting aspects for both the server side and the client side. For the server side, some of the topics include solving push contention with server-side rebasing (pushrebase), using scalable object storage for commits, moving various source control queries to the server, etc. For the client, there’s mention of the smartlog and other CLI commands for easier manipulation of history (compared to rebasing in Git).

However, more so than the technical aspects of the talk (which are interesting in their own right!), the main thing that has stayed with me throughout these years is the deep care for users that is reflected in Goode’s tone and words. It’s a bit difficult to convey this without the power of voice, You should watch the presentation!

but here are some quotes which reflect this:

In the context of hg smartlog : hg smartlog gives you a focused view of your branches and how they relate to the development trunk.

I know Git can produce this kind of UI if you know the incantation, but the critical thing here is not that it can be done; it’s that it becomes the default view of their source-control environment. That is where the power comes from: making it really intuitive for users to use source control and understand the concepts without reading a man page.

In the context of hg absorb : hg absorb auto-magically identifies the right commits in a stack to squash fixes into and rewrites history accordingly. This makes it easier to work with stacked changes.

This is the type of UI that we need to be inventing for our users: ones that match their intent and do it to the best of their ability, without making the user understand everything they have to do. It’s a little bit magic, but it’s magic in a very clean way. I think a lot of user experiences could benefit from this approach.

If you want to undo an amend or undo parts of a commit in Mercurial, you just run unamend and uncommit. You don’t have to understand a reflog; you don’t have to get a PhD to understand reset anymore. It just works, and it gives users confidence that they can recover from mistakes. That’s one of the most important things we can do: provide user experiences that give them confidence in what they’re doing.

On the user experience side, we as a source control community need to do a better job of building UIs that are accessible, intuitive, and that enable novice users to be power users. Everything I just talked about is how we are trying to do that for our users at Facebook. If the Git community could do that, the massive number of Git users taking advantage of it has the potential to redefine productivity for an entire generation of users.

Over the years, the possibility of these workflows lingered in my mind as I continued working with Git. I tried building my own wrappers on top of the git CLI to do some of these things, but I couldn’t get the performance to be reasonable…

items.title: Snap reaches settlement with two social media victims, avoiding trial
items.content:
The settlement resolves the cases of two unnamed plaintiffs, whose trial was set to begin on Wednesday.

LOS ANGELES (CN) — Snap Inc. reached a confidential settlement Monday with two plaintiffs who sued four major social media companies over mental health harms they say they suffered as teenagers, on the eve of trial.

The tech company, maker of the messaging app Snapchat, was the last remaining defendant in the bellwether trial, where jury selection was already underway.

The plaintiffs, identified in court as S.J., a female minor, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old woman, are among more than 2,000 people who say apps like Instagram, YouTube and TikTok caused them to become hopelessly addicted to their phones, leading to depression, anxiety and body dysmorphia.

“Families shouldn’t have to go jury by jury to solve a problem this big," said plaintiff’s attorney Mark Lanier in a written statement. “What these teenagers need is a permanent fix, real design changes that protect kids, not case-by-case patches. Until that happens, we will keep trying these cases.”

A Snap spokesman said in a written statement: “The Parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner.” She added: “Snapchat was built to encourage real conversations with real friends. We’ve built safeguards, launched safety tutorials, and partnered with experts and because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community.”

The other three defendants, Meta, Google and TikTok, had already reached confidential settlements with the two plaintiffs. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel were scheduled to testify at the trial, which was set to begin Wednesday.

The first bellwether trial, held earlier this year, ended with a jury awarding Kaley G.M. $6 million on her claims against Meta and Google after she had settled with Snap and TikTok. Meta and Google appealed, and those appeals are pending.

The next bellwether plaintiff, identified in court as R.K.C., settled with Google, TikTok and Snap before dropping the claims against Meta days before trial.

The next trials are scheduled to begin in March 2027.

Until recently, social media companies were largely shielded from liability by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which protects online platforms from lawsuits over third-party content. But plaintiffs in the consolidated youth social media cases successfully argued the companies could still be held liable for design features such as “likes,” autoplay and infinite scroll, which they say encourage teens to compulsively use the apps. They also targeted “beauty filters” on Instagram and Snapchat, which they say can cause or worsen body dysmorphia.

Snap also faces a lawsuit from the parents of more than 75 teens who died of fentanyl overdoses. The parents say their children bought drugs from dealers they met through Snapchat, which they call an “open-air drug market.”

items.title: Resisting Cognitive Surrender
items.content:
Working Notes: a commonplace notebook for recording & exploring ideas.

Home . Site Map . Subscribe . More at expLog .

This particular note is around exploring cognitive surrender : uncritically accepting whatever agents output without actually thinking , exploring or considering alternatives. Working this way is extremely fast, not particularly taxing, and unsurprisingly seductive.

And yet I find myself repeatedly questioning if this is actually a good way to apply agents: often enough I find myself making suboptimal decisions, accruing technical debt and reducing my familiarity with the system I’m working on instead of improving it.

As we collectively rethink how we work I’ve been finding it useful to read and share other people’s workflows, and consciously write about and examine my own. This particular post focuses on finding the right balance of trust while working with agents.

One of the virtues of being a great programmer is to be lazy . After more than a decade of training myself to look for the shortest and simplest path it’s rather attractive to be able to simply hand over the problem. If I can spin up a software factory, why wouldn’t I?

There’s also a lot of peer pressure (or game theory) at work: if any of my colleagues have seemingly surrendered, then I’m only going to look worse if I spend too much time trying to do silly things like understanding what I’m working on. And, of course , while everyone else is a slop-cannon generating code faster than they can read it I can build a meticulously designed software factory manufacturing perfect designs. The sheer volume of work also appears remarkably productive – we’ve all talked about just how many more PRs we ship every day.

This tends to get compounded by the agents’ expressed confidence & conviction. Perhaps an inadvertent consequence of RLHF, but models tend to be astonishingly confident in what they recommend (and perhaps even more blasé while admitting they made a mistake). This makes it too easy to take their answers at face value, with whatever social programming I seem to have evolved with.

OSS projects – particularly those facing time pressure – seem to accrue tremendous complexity quickly, to the point that it feels like the only way to interact with a project in any sane time frame is by heavily relying on agents to navigate and modify and test the code. This is also a self-reinforcing feedback loop: broken windows multiply rapidly with agents on the loose. [1]

Technical debt and incidental complexity have a fairly attenuated feedback loop: complexity introduced by slop doesn’t bite immediately; it’s far more subtle and compounds over time when I’m not paying attention.

Beyond all of that, I have to mention the hype cycle. We all should be skipping Netflix to watch talks by Anthropic engineers on making loops (or the agentic workflow du jour ). [2]

It’s not entirely obvious that it’s a bad idea to surrender: if it’s easier and better , then why not take that path? So far, my personal answer is that I need to take the easier path consciously and intentionally, with enough effort to mitigate downsides.

Part of what makes me deeply uncomfortable is suffering from a form of Gell-Mann amnesia while working with agents. When I have expertise and the overall design direction I can generally simplify the output significantly, controlling for complexity. When I don’t they seem to be the smartest engineers in existence – far beyond the more squishy, organic variety – and all I can do is follow in awe. And then the agent gets stuck creating a directory and I have to reset all my assumptions.

For the current state of the art (October 2026) I generally find maximal use of agents leads to a significant explosion in complexity: something that mostly works, with extremely surprising edge cases and bugs. These are generally the projects with hundreds of thousands of lines of code shipped rapidly, breaking the scale supported by most software development…

items.title: What are you doing this week?
items.content:
What are you doing this week? Feel free to share!

Keep in mind it’s OK to do nothing at all, too.

I got completely fed up with the direction of tech and cold quit just over a week ago. Last week was just recuperating from years of whatever the fork that was, this week I'm starting to look at what a next career might be while also getting some embargoed blog posts cleaned up I can finally post. I'm not really coding anything of import, though, and that's been very pleasant.

Wow. I don't have these kinds of balls. Hat tip for being ballzie. Best of luck on your next arc.

Any thoughts on where it might be? I'm always intrigued on what former programmer/tech people pivot to.

Tech was originally supposed to be the "temporary" career, so I've got some ideas, but I need to start by figuring out how feasible they are when I've got a family and an established community instead of a lone dude fresh out of college in my 20s. All of them are way more about people, way less about tech.

Buckle up. I did this back in May and haven't found anything better yet, which became more stressful, though in different ways, to be honest.

I poured everything into Uruky and that grew well over this period, but it's at 10-15% of the revenue we'd need. I've started focusing on other products recently, but very few people (and businesses) care enough to pay for well-built non-AI products that are privacy-focused.

I envy your ability to cold quit. I am also fairly burnt out, but don’t have the financial runway to quit.

I am also fairly burnt out, but don’t have the financial runway to quit.

I am sorry. To be very transparent, I spent years getting to where I could "just quit", but every single time I hit a goal of "I need to get at least $X amount of runway," I'd find some excuse why that still wasn't enough. I ended up torturing myself with jobs I didn't like and making sacrifices for work long after I honestly should've quit.

I know I'm extremely fortunate that I can do what I'm doing, but this is also kind of the reverse joke of overnight successes taking a decade: I was successful for a decade so I could be an overnight quitter.

(The fact that I genuinely enjoy computing and programming made this a lot harder; I basically got slow-boiled as tech stopping being punk, scrum became normal, the industry collectively opted for predictability over innovation/that innovation that did happen ended up being entirely about holding eyeballs, etc. For a lot of that, because of my seniority and careful choices, I almost got to pretend things hadn't changed. I just eventually hit a point where I couldn't pretend anymore. Probably a blog post in there when I've had a chance to convalesce a bit.)

Congrats. Some of us are too old to go anywhere else and I'm in that troupe.

Taking a full day off (5:45 AM - 10:30 PM) to run the polling place for my local elections. Also threw together a very simple website to support my project where kids vote just outside the actual election (voting for what kind of party to throw in the park 2 weeks later).

In theory I'm supposed to be writing a design document for work, describing some alternate approaches for storing certain data, but time is scarce and I'm concerned I won't have it written up in time because I'm taking time off to run elections and because my boss is assigning me additional work writing up my end-of-year evaluation (I am poor and slow at writing self-evaluations).

Thanks for your service! This is awesome.

I have to say, I love living in Washington where we can all just mail it in. I'm not even sure where I would go to vote in person anymore. I do not miss those days. I love having an hour to read the voters pamphlet, do other research, and hammer out my votes right at the kitchen table with my wife.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.summary_ko: YellowKey라는 제로데이 익스플로잇이 물리적 접근으로 Windows 11의 BitLocker를 우회해 암호화된 드라이브에 접근 가능하게 한다. 수 초 내에 보호를 무효화할 수 있다.
items.content_ko: 보안 연구자 Nightmare-Eclipse가 공개한 YellowKey 제로데이 취약점은 물리적 접근만으로 Windows 11 기본 BitLocker 보호를 우회할 수 있다. BitLocker는 Microsoft가 제공하는 전체 볼륨 암호화 기술로, 신뢰할 수 있는 플랫폼 모듈(TPM)에 저장된 복호화 키 없이는 디스크 접근이 불가능하도록 설계되었다. 많은 조직과 정부 계약업체에서 필수 보호 기술로 사용 중이다. YellowKey 익스플로잇의 핵심은 커스텀으로 만들어진 FsTx 폴더 사용으로, fstx.dll과 관련된 디렉터리는 Microsoft의 transactional NTFS 기술을 활용한다.

items.title: Supermarket Freezers Across Europe Hit With Another Cyberattack
items.content:
Supermarket refrigerators and freezers in at least a dozen European countries were hit with a cyberattack on Monday, following on the heels of similar attacks in France last month and U.S. military bases over the summer.

Stores in Ireland, Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, the Netherlands, Finland, and Estonia saw their refrigerators and freezers heated to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit), according to a report from the BBC . The attacks appear to have hit a large number of chains, including Ikea, Delhaize, Carrefour, and SuperValu, among others.

A few hours after this article was first published there were reports about refrigeration systems in other countries being attacked, including Germany , Portugal , Romania , and Italy .

It’s not clear who’s behind the attacks, but European officials have said they’re investigating. Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away after the attack in France last month, though it’s too early to tell what the economic cost may be this time.

Among the European countries where freezers have been hit Monday, Delhaize supermarket locations in Belgium and Luxembourg seem to be suffering the most. About 40 Delhaize supermarkets were attacked, according to the BBC, while there were fewer shops hit in Ireland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Finland, and Estonia.

Supermarkets allow their freezers to connect to the internet so that maintenance and monitoring can occur remotely. Early reports suggest that some of the refrigeration units targeted on Monday were made by a Danish firm called Danfoss, according to Reuters, which were also targeted in France last month.

Patrick Lamplmair, CTO at the Austria-based cybersecurity firm Tributech, told Gizmodo that assets connected to the internet need to be checked for exposure to hackers, no matter how mundane, especially if there have been previous attacks.

“Reports point to known flaws in refrigeration controllers that already had fixes, and thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack, said Lamplmair. “There is no data to steal and no ransom to negotiate. A few commands to a temperature controller destroy stock overnight and close stores.”

Lamplmair also suggested there should be some common sense involved in how these systems are designed. “A freezer should never accept an instruction to heat to 50°C, no matter who sends it,” said Lamplmair.

The U.S. military is still investigating what’s believed to be a coordinated cyberattack on refrigeration systems at American bases in late August. Military commissaries in California, New Mexico, George, Rhode Island, and others were affected .

Katrien Eggers, a spokesperson for Belgium’s Center for Cybersecurity, told Reuters that it’s not known who orchestrated the attack on European supermarkets and the culprit may never be known. Eggers said she was concerned about the rise of AI, which has supercharged the ability of bad actors to attack infrastructure and commerce.

“All IT systems are potentially vulnerable, and AI can now be used to successfully exploit these weaknesses— especially by sophisticated actors,” said Eggers.

There’s a heightened awareness in the cybersecurity space that everything is more vulnerable right now. Between Russia’s war in Ukraine and President Donald Trump’s pledge to restart major bombing in Iran, there are plenty of incentives for a host of actors to target major infrastructure around the world.

Ukraine and Russia both reported major cyberattacks on their emergency alert systems Monday, with residents of Kyiv getting “nuclear danger” alerts through an air raid app on Sunday, according to Bloomberg . Russia’s Emergencies Ministry app was hacked just a couple of hours later, according to CBS News.

items.title: Gitea 28.3.0 is released
items.content:
We are excited to announce the release of Gitea 28.3.0 , the third maintenance release for the 28 series. It contains a large number of security fixes, mostly around token scopes, and bug fixes and performance improvements for Actions, issues, pull requests and packages. We strongly recommend that all users upgrade as soon as possible.

This release addresses the following security vulnerabilities. Please upgrade as soon as possible.

We are grateful to all the security researchers who responsibly disclosed these issues.

This release includes 60 merged pull requests , thanks to the amazing contributions from our community.

Download our pre-built binaries from the Gitea downloads page — make sure to select the version compatible with your platform. For a step-by-step guide on installation or upgrades, check out our installation documentation .

We would also like to thank all of our supporters on Open Collective who are helping to sustain us financially.

Gitea is open source. Star our GitHub repo, and join our community on Discord!
items.title_ko: Gitea 28.3.0 출시
items.summary_ko: Gitea 28.3.0이 출시됐으며, 이번 릴리스는 주로 토큰 스코프 관련 다수의 보안 수정을 담고 있다. Actions, 이슈, 풀 리퀘스트, 패키지 관련 버그 수정과 성능 개선도 포함됐고, 모든 사용자에게 가능한 한 빨리 업그레이드를 권장했다.
items.content_ko: Gitea 28 시리즈의 세 번째 유지보수 릴리스인 28.3.0이 출시됐다. 토큰 스코프(token scopes) 관련 보안 수정이 대부분을 차지하며, Actions, 이슈, 풀 리퀘스트, 패키지 관련 버그 수정과 성능 개선도 포함됐다. 이번 릴리스에는 커뮤니티가 기여한 병합된 풀 리퀘스트 60건이 들어갔다. 개발팀은 모든 사용자가 가능한 한 빨리 업그레이드할 것을 강력히 권장했고, 보안 취약점을 책임 있게 공개한 연구자들에게 감사를 표했다. 사전 빌드된 바이너리는 다운로드 페이지에서 받을 수 있으며, 설치와 업그레이드 절차는 설치 문서를 참고하라고 안내했다.

items.title: 사생활침해 범죄가 의심 됩니다. 도움이 필요합니다
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-89229 📢 Source: Vivo 💣 CVSS Score: 5.1 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') in the ShareActivity component of BlueLM Copilot (com.vivo.ai.copilot) allows a malicious application installed on the same device to write arbitrary files via a crafted ACTION_SEND intent with a ContentProvider-supplied file name containing '..' sequences. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-03T09:46:55.368Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-89229
items.title_ko: BlueLM Copilot ShareActivity의 경로 순회 취약점 (CVE-2026-89229)
items.summary_ko: Vivo BlueLM Copilot의 ShareActivity 컴포넌트에 경로 순회 취약점이 있어, 같은 기기에 설치된 악성 앱이 조작된 인텐트로 임의 파일을 쓸 수 있다. CVSS 5.1(MEDIUM)이며, 원격 공격 가능 여부는 False로 표시됐다.
items.content_ko: Vivo의 BlueLM Copilot(com.vivo.ai.copilot)에 있는 ShareActivity 컴포넌트에서 경로를 제한 디렉터리로 제대로 제한하지 않아 경로 순회(Path Traversal) 취약점이 존재한다. 같은 기기에 설치된 악성 앱이 ContentProvider가 제공하는 파일 이름에 '..' 시퀀스를 포함한 조작된 ACTION_SEND 인텐트를 보내 임의의 파일을 쓸 수 있다. CVSS 점수는 5.1(MEDIUM)이며, 원격 공격 가능(Remotely Exploitable: False)으로는 표시되지 않았다. 공개일은 2026-11-03이다.
